operation_trace.defect_title: Divergent definition of 'viable' / viability certification mechanics vs. 60-day suspension trigger

operation.parameters: Annotate Reg A OBL-14's viability-suspension pathway as implementing 12 USC 347b(b)(2), and mark the statutory certification-timing structure (347b-5: '60-day period beginning on the date such certification is received', renewable) as its authoritative source; flag the regulation's 'or after consultation with the Board of Governors' clause as a divergence lacking a corresponding statutory suspension trigger.
operation.proposal: Establish an explicit cross-reference linking Reg A OBL-14 (the undercapitalized-institution viability relief) to its statutory parent 12 USC 347b(b)(2)/347b-5, so the blueprint records that the regulatory suspension mechanism derives from and is bounded by the statutory certification-timing structure. The link surfaces the material difference: the statute keys the 60-day suspension to 'the date such certification is received' with renewable 60-day extensions, whereas the regulation frames relief as available during 60 days after receipt of certification OR 'after consultation with the Board of Governors' — an alternative pathway with no counterpart in the statutory suspension text.
operation.rationale: This is a drawing-fix, not a brick-fix: the two provisions govern the same relief but the blueprint currently presents them as freestanding, obscuring the parent-child relationship and the divergence. RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE makes the dependency explicit without altering either requirement. It does NOT resolve the substantive divergence (the 'consultation with the Board' pathway): P3.5 newest-wins cannot be invoked because there is no explicit supersession in the sources — the statute does not state that the regulation may add pathways, and the regulation does not claim to supersede the statute. Whether the regulatory 'consultation' pathway is a permissible gloss or an ultra vires expansion is a policy/legal question outside the refactor pass; it is flagged here for the Redesign Backlog, not silently reconciled.

draft_classification.baseline_reasoning: Hierarchy and delegation: 12 U.S.C. 347b is the controlling statute, while Regulation A implements Federal Reserve lending authority under delegated rulemaking authority. For the Federal Reserve Bank cell, 347b-4 and 347b-5 establish the 60-days-in-120 limitation and the operative exception: suspension begins when the Reserve Bank receives a written viability certification and may be renewed through additional certifications. Regulation A OBL-14 addresses the same undercapitalized-institution lending activity, so the baseline supports recording the parent-child cross-reference and treating the statute as hierarchically authoritative. Applicability and status controls align around advances to an undercapitalized insured depository institution and current, verified statutory and regulatory text. For the certifying-official cell, the statute specifies certification by the appropriate federal banking agency head or, following a Board examination, the Board Chairman, and prohibits delegation; this supports identifying written certification as the statutory trigger. For the Board-consultation cell, Regulation A's alternative 'after consultation with the Board of Governors' pathway lacks a corresponding trigger in the supplied statutory suspension text. The baseline therefore supports flagging a divergence but is ambiguous about its legal consequence: the sources do not establish whether consultation is a permissible regulatory implementation or an unauthorized expansion. Because the operation only adds the cross-reference and preserves that ambiguity rather than reconciling or changing either provision, it clarifies the existing baseline rather than changing it. It is not fill_gap because no preexisting actor duty is newly made explicit, and not codify because the regulation-statute fit is materially ambiguous at the consultation pathway. Human classification remains required.

operation_trace.defect_title: Divergent definitions of 'insolvent' for emergency-lending purposes

operation.parameters: Canonical anchor: the statutory definition at 12 USC 343(3)(B)(ii) ('A borrower shall be considered insolvent for purposes of this subparagraph, if the borrower is in bankruptcy, resolution under title II of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, or any other Federal or State insolvency proceeding.'). Regulation A's paragraph (d) definition of 'insolvent' is marked as a distinct, broader regulatory term rather than a restatement of the same term.
operation.proposal: Record at blueprint level that the term 'insolvent' carries two distinct definitions across the two sources: a statutory definition (bankruptcy / Title II resolution / any other Federal or State insolvency proceeding) and a materially broader Regulation A definition (which adds the '90-day undisputed-debts' test and a residual Board/Reserve-Bank determination). The move canonicalizes the statutory text as the anchor definition and flags the Reg A definition as a divergent, wider variant of the same lexical term rather than silently treating the two as one definition. It does NOT collapse them into one meaning — doing so would change what the law requires.
operation.rationale: This is a refactor-pass drawing fix: the blueprint currently shows a single term 'insolvent' with conflicting content, which misrepresents the sources. CANONICALIZE-DEFINITION makes the definitional relationship explicit and picks the statutory text as the anchor, without altering either instrument's operative meaning. Critically, P3.5 newest-wins does NOT resolve the conflict here: the statute expressly delegates to the Board the power to 'establish procedures to prohibit borrowing from programs and facilities by borrowers that are insolvent,' so the broader Reg A definition may be a lawful exercise of delegated authority rather than an ultra vires expansion the blueprint may override. There is no explicit supersession of the statutory definition by the regulation — the statute confines its own definition to 'for purposes of this subparagraph.' Therefore choosing which definition governs is a POLICY CHOICE, not a mechanical newest-wins outcome; this operation only records the divergence and anchors the statutory text, leaving substantive reconciliation to the Redesign program.

citations.quote: A borrower shall be considered insolvent for purposes of this subparagraph, if the borrower is in bankruptcy, resolution under title II of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act
The person or entity is generally not paying its undisputed debts as they become due during the 90 days preceding the date of borrowing under the program or facility; or
The Board shall establish procedures to prohibit borrowing from programs and facilities by borrowers that are insolvent.

draft_classification.baseline_reasoning: The operative baseline already requires preserving the two source-specific definitions rather than collapsing them. At the hierarchy and delegation level, 12 U.S.C. § 343(3)(B)(ii) supplies an express definition limited to “purposes of this subparagraph,” while § 343 separately directs the Board to establish procedures prohibiting insolvent borrowers. Regulation A paragraph (d), issued under that delegation, requires a Federal Reserve Bank to obtain evidence that a prospective borrower is not insolvent and applies a definition that includes the statutory proceeding-based conditions plus the 90-day undisputed-debts and residual Board/Reserve-Bank-determination tests. Both sources are applicable to § 13(3) broad-based emergency-lending programs, but they occupy different hierarchical levels and contain facially different criteria. Current-law status controls therefore require the blueprint to retain the enacted statutory text as the canonical statutory anchor and separately represent the final regulation’s broader wording. The operation does not decide whether the additional regulatory tests are a valid delegated implementation, alter borrower eligibility, or supersede the statutory definition; it records the divergence and prevents an inaccurate merger. Because that representational output follows directly from the operative source texts, the effect is codify rather than change or unresolved. It is not fill_gap: no omitted duty is being inferred from another source, and the operation adds no new duty.

operation.parameters: Canonical definition anchor = 12 USC 343(3)(A) as elaborated by 12 USC 343(3)(A)(iii). The statute supplies only the negative/exclusionary content ('shall not be considered ...'); Regulation A supplies the affirmative content ('designed to provide liquidity to an identifiable market or sector of the financial system') and a quantitative floor ('fewer than five persons/entities'). Canonicalize by recording ONE definition record for the term whose content is the UNION of both instruments' contributions, with each fragment attributed to its source instrument, rather than two competing free-standing definitions.
operation.proposal: Register a single canonical definition entry for the term 'program or facility with broad-based eligibility' that is layered: (a) statutory exclusion (single-and-specific-company structures excluded), (b) regulatory affirmative criterion (designed to provide liquidity to an identifiable market or sector), and (c) regulatory quantitative exclusion (fewer-than-five eligibles). Each layer carries a source tag so the reader sees that the affirmative and quantitative content originates in Regulation A, not the statute. This replaces the current picture of 'same term, two divergent definitions' with one definition composed of source-attributed layers.
operation.rationale: This is a fix-the-drawing move: the underlying legal content is not being changed, only how the definition is represented. The statute defines the term only negatively and, per the extraction, is 'Not affirmatively defined'; Regulation A adds affirmative and quantitative content. Reg A is expressly the instrument the statute directs to fill in the operative detail ('shall be subject to such limitations, restrictions, and regulations as the Board of Governors ... may prescribe' and 'the Board shall establish, by regulation ... the policies and procedures governing emergency lending under this paragraph'), so the two are not true peers in conflict — the regulation is the statutorily-contemplated elaboration. Canonicalizing them into one layered record is meaning-preserving. NOTE: this treats Reg A's fewer-than-five quantitative floor as a permissible elaboration of the statutory grant rather than a conflict; if an Authority reads the quantitative floor as adding a substantive limit the statute does not authorize, that is a substantive question outside the refactor pass and must route to the Redesign Backlog.

draft_classification.baseline_reasoning: The current U.S. federal baseline already requires the layered substantive result represented by the operation. At the statutory level, 12 U.S.C. § 343(3)(A) authorizes emergency lending only through a program or facility with broad-based eligibility and excludes structures directed at assisting a single and specific company. The statute also subjects such lending to Board-prescribed limitations, restrictions, and regulations and directs the Board, in consultation with the Treasury Secretary, to establish governing policies and procedures by regulation. Exercising that delegation, final Regulation A supplies the affirmative market-or-sector criterion and the fewer-than-five eligibility exclusion. These regulatory layers apply to § 343(3) programs; they are not represented as statutory text and must retain their regulatory source attribution. Thus, for each touched cell, an operative program must satisfy the statute and the applicable Regulation A criteria cumulatively. A single source-layered record does not alter eligibility, authority, actors, triggers, or legal hierarchy; it codifies the combined current-law baseline while preventing the regulatory elaborations from being misattributed to Congress. No fill-gap rationale is needed because the operation creates no new duty and does not merely make an independently sourced actor duty explicit. The possible legal-validity objection to the fewer-than-five rule is not resolved by this refactor, but the supplied baseline contains no contrary controlling authority or status defect that makes the current operative rule indeterminate. operation_trace.defect_title: Applicability threshold divergence for lending to undercapitalized vs critically undercapitalized institutions

operation.rationale: The defect (D10) reads as a divergence, but the drawing already contains the fork: OBL-5 requires the Reserve Bank to determine which of the two statuses applies and then follow the § 201.5 procedures. The two windows are branches keyed to distinct source-defined states, not conflicting rules over the same state. RELATE-OBLIGATION makes that parent/branch structure explicit and meaning-preserving. draft_classification.baseline_reasoning: The current federal regulatory baseline already establishes the proposed parent/branch relationship. Reg A directs a Federal Reserve Bank, before extending credit, to determine whether the borrower is an undercapitalized or critically undercapitalized insured depository institution and, if either status applies, to follow § 201.5. OBL-14 and OBL-15 then prescribe different lending windows for those mutually differentiated capitalization statuses: no more than 60 days outstanding in any 120-day period for an undercapitalized institution, and a 5-day period beginning when an institution becomes critically undercapitalized. Their applicability is controlled by the same section 38 FDI Act capitalization classification invoked through OBL-5. The operation therefore records the hierarchy and conditional structure already expressed by operative, current regulation; it does not alter an actor, trigger, status definition, modality, exception, or time window. The wording of OBL-5 uses “should,” but that does not make the branch relationship indeterminate: the distinct status-triggered restrictions remain operative once their respective conditions apply. Treating the two provisions as sibling branches is thus meaning-preserving codification rather than a new duty or policy reconciliation. Human confirmation remains required because the baseline_set_for resolver is not implemented.

operation_trace.defect_title: Full discount-window operational-readiness obligation assembled only across multiple instruments

operation.parameters: Consolidate the fragments of the discount-window operational-readiness duty into a single composite obligation carried on the addendum (the source that supplies the operative 'operational readiness' definition), cross-linked from the OCC bulletin and FDIC FIL as transmitting instruments. Composite duty: where the discount window is part of the CFP, the institution should (a) understand the discount-window requirements [OCC 'understand requirements'], (b) establish borrowing arrangements and ensure collateral is available in an amount appropriate to potential contingency needs [addendum ob-9 / FDIC OB-5], (c) be familiar with the pledging process for different collateral types and aware of the utility of pre-pledging [addendum ob-10], (d) consider conducting small-value transactions at regular intervals for familiarity [addendum], and (e) be aware of operational requirements and test access on a regular basis [FDIC OB-4].
operation.proposal: Merge the scattered operational-readiness fragments into one composite discount-window operational-readiness obligation anchored on the addendum, which supplies the definitional core ('Operational readiness includes...'), with the OCC 'understand requirements' framing and the FDIC collateral-availability/testing components folded in as constituent elements rather than free-standing partial statements. The merge is meaning-preserving: no element is dropped, strengthened, or weakened, and each retains its own citation.
operation.rationale: D7 is a drawing defect, not a bricks defect: the duty already exists in full across the sources but no single node states it. MERGE assembles the constituent 'should' obligations into one blueprint obligation so a reader sees the complete duty in one place. The addendum is the correct anchor because it alone defines 'operational readiness' and supplies the pledging/small-value elements; the OCC and FDIC fragments are the same duty stated at lower granularity. All merged fragments share actor (depository institutions), modality (should/conditional-on-CFP-inclusion), and the same conditional trigger ('if the discount window is part of the CFP'), so no conflict resolution under P3.5 is required. No new duty is created, so ADR-005 is not triggered.

Depository institutions should ensure they are familiar with the pledging process for different collateral types and be aware that pre-pledging collateral can be useful if liquidity needs arise quickly. draft_classification.baseline_reasoning: The current baseline supports every constituent element, but it does not state the proposed composite with one unambiguous applicability rule. The interagency addendum supplies the definitional core: if the discount window is part of a depository institution’s CFP, the institution should establish and maintain operational readiness, including borrowing arrangements and appropriately sized available collateral. It separately states pledging-process and pre-pledging expectations and says institutions with the window in their CFP should consider regular small-value transactions. The OCC bulletin applies to national banks, federal savings associations, and federal branches and agencies of foreign banking organizations and adds the conditional expectation to understand facility requirements. The FDIC FIL applies to FDIC-supervised institutions and states general contingent-source testing and collateral expectations. These are supervisory guidance or transmitting instruments, so their existing nonbinding modalities and qualifications—especially “should,” “should consider,” and the CFP trigger—must be preserved; the merge cannot convert them into a mandatory rule. Applicability is not perfectly coextensive: the OCC and FDIC statements govern their respective supervised populations, while the addendum speaks to depository institutions; moreover, the FDIC testing language concerns contingent sources generally, and the addendum’s pledging language is not expressly subject to the CFP trigger. Thus the baseline supports the consolidated presentation, but ambiguity remains about actor coverage, activity-specific triggers, and whether general contingent-source expectations are discount-window-specific. The operation is therefore a clarification rather than fill_gap or change, provided the composite retains each element’s original scope, modality, trigger, and citation rather than imposing one common trigger or duty strength.

operation.parameters: Draw an explicit relation between OBL-1 (advance must be secured to the Reserve Bank's satisfaction) and OBL-3 (Reserve Bank must keep itself informed of the general character and amount of the loans and investments of a depository institution) as the two blueprint anchors that jointly presuppose visibility into FHLB-pledged assets.
operation.proposal: At blueprint level, record an explicit relation between OBL-1 and OBL-3: the duty to secure the advance 'to the satisfaction of the Federal Reserve Bank' is informed by the standing duty to keep informed of the character and amount of the institution's loans and investments. Naming this relation makes visible that neither obligation, as drawn, reaches the FHLB collateral/operational rules governing the same assets — which is the fragmentation D9 identifies. This is a drawing fix: it clarifies how existing obligations connect, without changing what either requires.
operation.rationale: D9 is fundamentally a missing-relation defect: two Reg A obligations (secure to satisfaction; keep informed of loans/investments) together imply the Reserve Bank needs a full picture of an institution's collateral, yet the blueprint shows no edge to the FHLB regime that co-governs that collateral. RELATE-OBLIGATION is the whitelist-legitimate way to expose that gap on the drawing without inventing a substantive coordination rule. It changes no requirement (P3 refactor constraint) and is advisory per ADR-003.

Keep itself informed of the general character and amount of the loans and investments of a depository institution as provided in section 4(8) of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 301); and

draft_classification.baseline_reasoning: Current operative federal law supplies both endpoints but does not expressly state the proposed relationship. Regulation A requires the Federal Reserve Bank making an advance to secure it to its satisfaction (OBL-1), and separately requires the Bank to remain informed of the general character and amount of a depository institution’s loans and investments and to consider that information when deciding whether to extend credit (OBL-3), with OBL-3 cross-referencing 12 U.S.C. 301. Their common actor, applicability to Reserve Bank credit decisions, and placement in the same operative regime support reading institution-level asset information as relevant to the secured-advance decision. The baseline is nevertheless ambiguous about whether OBL-3 specifically informs the OBL-1 collateral-satisfaction determination; it does not expressly identify FHLB-pledged status, FHLB collateral rules, interoperability, or information exchange. No identified status control alters that result. Accordingly, a blueprint edge limited to showing a supported connection between existing duties is a clarification, not a new operative requirement. The edge must not state or imply that current law mandates visibility into FHLB pledges or coordination with FHLBs: that stronger proposition is absent from the supplied baseline and would route as change. Human confirmation is warranted because the operation’s phrase “presuppose visibility into FHLB-pledged assets” could be read either as a diagnostic inference or as an asserted legal requirement.

The defect is that 'discount-window stigma' is a material scope term the ratified scope requires cataloguing, yet the source text (12 CFR Part 201, Regulation A) contains no substantive definition or treatment of it — only a closest verbatim anchor about advances and discounting. SUBSTITUTE-TERM is unavailable because there is no synonymous term in the source to substitute (strict meaning-preservation would be violated). INTRODUCE under ADR-005 is limited to making explicit a duty the sources already establish; 'discount-window stigma' is a diagnostic/analytic concept, not an obligation, so INTRODUCE does not reach it. The honest diagnosis: 'discount-window stigma' is not a defined or regulated term within Regulation A at all — it is a structural/behavioral phenomenon the ratified scope asks the program to CATALOGUE from evidence, not a blueprint element that Regulation A left undefined. The verified anchor ('A Federal Reserve Bank may lend to a depository institution either by making an advance secured by acceptable collateral under § 201.4 of this part or by discounting certain types of paper.') confirms the discount-window mechanism exists in the source but says nothing about stigma. This is therefore a scope/evidence-sourcing gap, not a refactorable drawing defect: the term's substantive content must come from a definitional source outside the excerpted Regulation A text (e.g., the reform-proposal or stigma-catalogue sources the scope contemplates), and its treatment belongs in the diagnostic catalogue the program is chartered to produce — not in a blueprint edit to 12 CFR Part 201. Recommend routing to the Redesign/diagnostic backlog with a logged finding: (1) the Derived Blueprint should not record 'discount-window stigma' as an 'undefined-here' element of 12-cfr-201-reg-a, because the term is not an element of that source; and (2) an ADR is warranted to establish where cross-source analytic/diagnostic terms (as opposed to source-internal defined terms) are to be defined and cited, since the whitelist provides no operation for supplying a definition absent from every excerpted source.

The refactor pass can only make the inconsistency visible (NORMALIZE-ELEMENTS) and structurally explained (RELATE-OBLIGATION); harmonizing it is a Principal-led redesign decision.

The whitelist cannot express the substantive fix the defect ultimately points toward: aligning the FHLB curtailment/transition trigger with the Fed-side PCA/CAMELS-5 and capital-standard thresholds so the same distressed institution faces a coherent hand-off point. That is a threshold-harmonization across two independently chartered regimes — it would change what the instruments require (or newly bind FHFA/FHLBanks to statutory Fed categories) and is neither meaning-preserving (barred in the refactor pass) nor supported by any explicit supersession between the sources (P3.5). RECALIBRATE is available in the enum but would alter the operative threshold and thus exceeds ADR-003's advisory/blueprint boundary and the refactor-pass mandate. Logging as a candidate ADR / Redesign Backlog item: 'Harmonize FHLB member-credit-distress triggers with Federal Reserve undercapitalization/supervisory-rating thresholds governing the discount-window transition,' to be taken up by the Principal-led redesign program.

The core remedy a reader might want here — HARMONIZING the three applicability thresholds and cadences onto a common scoping basis — is not expressible by any P3.1 whitelist move. RECALIBRATE would change a threshold/cadence value (a substantive change to what the law requires), which the refactor pass forbids; NORMALIZE-ELEMENTS operates on the structural shape of like elements, not on divergent substantive threshold values set by distinct rulemakings (Regulation YY/LL categories vs. FFIEC universal filing vs. 12 CFR 201.2 discount-window scope). Choosing one common threshold/cadence would be a policy choice among non-superseding live sources (P3.5), and imposing it would be operative rule-design (ADR-003). This belongs to the separately-chartered Principal-led redesign program, not the diagnostic refactor. Logged as a candidate ADR: 'Common liquidity-detection scoping datum' — requires a Mandate objective and threshold-selection authority the refactor pass does not hold.

The whitelist can map and make explicit the divergent scopes (DEFINE-TERM, RELATE-OBLIGATION) but cannot RESOLVE the applicability-scope mismatch itself — i.e., decide which single population should govern a given obligation. Doing so would require harmonizing three co-live scope statements where no source contains an explicit supersession clause; under P3.5 that is a policy choice, not a meaning-preserving refactor. The MERGE move is inapposite because the three scopes are not duplicative expressions of one rule but genuinely different populations, so merging would silently change what the law reaches. A substantive reconciliation of the addressed populations should be logged for the Redesign Backlog rather than attempted in the refactor pass.

The whitelist can make the two thresholds' distinct domains legible, but it cannot HARMONIZE them into a single reconciled scoping regime if the Authority ultimately wants one threshold to govern both instruments. Choosing a unified threshold (or subordinating one to the other) is a substantive policy decision that changes what the instruments require and is barred by the refactor-pass mandate and ADR-003; P3.5 newest-wins does not apply because neither source explicitly supersedes the other. If genuine reconciliation is desired, this should be logged as a finding routed to the Redesign Backlog, not expressed as a P3.1 move.

The whitelist can canonicalize the phrasing (DEFINE-TERM) and record the genus/species relationship (RELATE-OBLIGATION), but it CANNOT resolve whether 'all large depository members' (OB-4) and 'large depository institution members' (OB-3) denote the same population or an intentionally different one, nor whether either carries an implied size threshold. No source text supplies a threshold or a supersession statement, so newest-wins (P3.5) does not apply and any harmonization of the scope itself would be a policy choice about what the law requires — outside the refactor pass and ADR-003. Recommend logging a Defect Register item routing the scope-reconciliation decision to the Principal-led Redesign program.

The whitelist can express the *structural* fix (relating the two obligations as branches of one status-keyed scheme), and that is what D10 actually needs at blueprint level, since the 'divergence' resolves to two source-distinct capitalization states rather than a genuine conflict over one state. What the whitelist cannot express — and should not, in a refactor pass — is any judgment that the 60-day vs 5-day asymmetry is itself defective and ought to be harmonized. RECALIBRATE exists in the op enum but is out of scope for P3.2/P3.1 (it would change what the law requires, violating the 'fix the drawing, not the bricks' rule) and is unavailable absent an adopted Mandate objective. If a reviewer believes the substantive window divergence (not its legibility) is the true defect, that is a policy finding for the separately chartered Redesign program, not a refactor move; log it there rather than improvising a scope-window edit here. Note also that P3.5 newest-wins offers no resolution: the two windows are not conflicting live sources but co-valid provisions, so no supersession applies.

The defect ultimately points to a substantive gap — firms outside the Category I-IV panel have no sub-quarterly liquidity reporting obligation, which bears on run-detection speed. Closing that gap (e.g., extending sub-quarterly liquidity reporting to smaller banks) would be a NEW duty, not one the sources establish, so INTRODUCE is unavailable under ADR-005 and no whitelist move can create it in the refactor pass. The refactor can only make the gap visible (done above); the remedy is a policy choice for the separately chartered Principal-led redesign program and should be routed to the Redesign Backlog. Note also FR2052A-OB-5 gives the Board discretionary authority to require more frequent data from monthly filers during stress, but that authority does not reach non-panel firms — reinforcing that the coverage floor is a substantive, not drawing, matter.

The whitelist can relate the existing fragments but cannot create the single authoritative instrument that states the full FHLB→discount-window transition duty in one place — that would require either a genuinely new consolidated duty (barred by ADR-005 as new law, hence a Redesign Backlog item) or a supersession choice among instruments that the sources do not explicitly authorize (P3.5: no explicit supersession exists among an FHFA guidance, an interagency addendum, and a pending bill, so consolidating them would be a policy choice, not a refactor). The move 'designate a home instrument for the assembled duty' is therefore not expressible at refactor level and should be logged for the Redesign program.

The relation cluster makes the scattered transition duty legible, but the underlying legibility gap the defect identifies — that no single provision states a consolidated, single-actor transition obligation — cannot be closed by any whitelist move without either (a) a MERGE that would flatten genuinely distinct FHFA vs FHLBank actors/modalities (meaning-changing, out of scope for the refactor pass), or (b) an INTRODUCE of a new consolidated duty that the sources do not establish as a single obligation. Under ADR-005 such a consolidated duty would be NEW, not merely made explicit, so it is not proposed here; it should be logged to the Redesign Backlog as a candidate for the separately chartered redesign program. RELATE-OBLIGATION is the honest ceiling of the refactor pass for D7.

The defect D5 concerns a lettering gap in the codified statute: 12 USC 1430 has no subsection (f), and the OLRC-preserved footnote records this. No P3.1 whitelist move can honestly resolve this at blueprint level. RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE is the closest candidate, but it presupposes an actual cross-reference whose target is misidentified or ambiguous; the extractions and source text excerpts contain no obligation or provision within 12 USC 1430 that cross-references a subsection (f). The obligations extracted (O1-O9) reference 'this section', 'section 1431(g)', 'paragraph (3)', and 'subparagraphs (D) and (E)' — none point to (f). The dangling slot is an artifact of the codification's alphabetical lettering (subsections (a)-(e) are present in the excerpt), not a live dangling reference from one provision to another. The available excerpt ends at subsection (e) and does not itself surface the footnote text or any provision citing (f), so no VERBATIM span establishing a resolvable cross-reference exists to cite. Correcting a lettering gap in the codified text would (1) be a fix to the bricks, not the drawing — outside the refactor pass mandate ('fix the drawing, not the bricks'), and (2) risk altering what the law's structure represents, which the refactor pass forbids. This is a logged finding recommending an ADR: the blueprint should carry an explicit annotation that the (f) slot is a codification artifact with no enacted content and no live inbound reference, and that any downstream extraction encountering it must treat it as intentionally void rather than a broken link. That annotation capability is not among the P3.1 whitelist moves, so nothing is proposed here.

The whitelist can type and flag the dangling reference but cannot itself acquire the missing 2024 Act text into the corpus, nor authoritatively establish the succession/supersession relationship between the 2024 Act and the 2026 bill. The source asserts temporal priority ('first introduced ... in 2024') but no explicit supersession, so no supersession edge is warranted here. Bringing the 2024 instrument into scope is a corpus-acquisition/scoping decision for the Authority, not a P3.1 refactor move.

The whitelist can bind/flag dangling references but cannot INGEST the missing off-page content (Collateral Eligibility page, Pledging Collateral page, Loan Types and Call Report Mapping Table, Historical Collateral Margins Tables page). Actually pulling those resources into the corpus is an extraction/scope action outside P3.1's refactor moves; the EXTERNAL-UNRESOLVED flags here should route to the extraction backlog, not be treated as fully resolved by these operations.

The defect is a dangling cross-reference: OB-14 (and the consolidation-floor discussion) point to 'the exceptions described above' governing the statutory floor that FHLBank districts not be reduced to fewer than eight, but the referenced exceptions do not appear in the excerpted extraction. The P3.1 whitelist move for a dangling reference is RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE — but that move requires a resolvable referent: an existing element (the described exceptions) to which the pointer can be re-bound. In the SOURCE TEXT EXCERPTS provided, the source text ends at the Executive Summary opening and never reaches Section V (Operational Efficiency, Structure, and Governance) or any text discussing district consolidation, the eight-district floor, or its exceptions. Therefore there is no VERBATIM span available to cite that establishes what 'the exceptions described above' are. RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE cannot be honestly proposed without inventing or guessing the referent, which would violate the machine-checked verbatim-quote rule and the ADR-003 prohibition on drafting text. Nor can INTRODUCE be used: the exceptions are a substantive statutory carve-out, and introducing them from nothing would be fabricating source content, not making explicit a duty the sources already establish. Recommended handling: this finding is not resolvable within the current extraction window. It should be routed back for a re-extraction that captures the Section V / consolidation-floor passage containing the actual exception language, after which a RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE (re-binding the OB-14 pointer to the now-present exception element) or, if the exceptions prove genuinely absent from the source document itself, a logged finding that the source's own cross-reference is dangling. Logging this as a scope/extraction-coverage gap, not an improvised edit.

The whitelist cannot express 'supply/verify a missing external statutory citation.' RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE can flag the reference as unresolved and route a resolution request, but it cannot itself identify the statute (e.g., 12 U.S.C. § 1442 or successor) because that provision is not present in the excerpted sources and importing it would violate the verbatim-quote rule and the refactor-pass constraint against changing the bricks. Actually resolving the citation requires source retrieval outside P3.1 — this belongs to the Authority as a citation-resolution / provenance task. The extraction quote is also flagged verified:false, so even the host assertion needs source verification before any downstream binding.
proposal for RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE rejected: 0/1 citation quotes verified

The whitelist can flag and type the cross-reference (RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE) but cannot reproduce the definiens of 'covered depository institution holding company' because the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio rules are not among the excerpted source texts. Fully resolving the reference — i.e., CANONICALIZE-DEFINITION or DEFINE-TERM with actual definitional content — requires ingesting the LCR/NSFR rule text into the corpus. Recommend logging a source-ingestion request rather than improvising the definition, since inventing definitional text would violate the VERBATIM-quote and meaning-preservation constraints.

The residual core of the defect — whether the Reg A one-year sunset, five-entity-minimum framing, and affirmative broad-based definition SUBSTANTIVELY SUPERSEDE the bare statutory grant that the CARES construction note purports to preserve 'as of the day before ... enactment' — cannot be resolved by any whitelist move. Under P3.5, newest-wins applies only where supersession is EXPLICIT in the sources; here the statute's preserved-baseline note and the regulation's added constraints are not reconciled by explicit supersession language in either text. Which instrument governs where they diverge (e.g. whether a constraint present in Reg A but absent from the preserved 13(3) baseline binds) is a policy choice, not a drafting cleanup. RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE and RELATE-OBLIGATION can only expose the linkage and derivation; they cannot adjudicate the baseline-vs-overlay conflict. This should be logged for the Redesign Backlog as a conflict-resolution question for the chartered Principal-led program, and it may warrant an ADR on how the blueprint represents a statutory preserved-baseline construction note that coexists with a more-constrained delegated-regulation restatement absent explicit supersession.

The whitelist cannot cleanly express the actual fix the defect implies — updating a statutory reference from an abolished office to its Dodd-Frank successor — because SUBSTITUTE-TERM is limited to strictly meaning-preserving renames and the correct successor here is a contested legal determination, not a mechanical one. Determining and inserting the successor officer is either operative legal text (barred by ADR-003) or a policy choice about Dodd-Frank function transfer (barred from silent resolution by P3.5, since no explicit supersession of 1430(h) is in the sources). This should be logged as a finding proposing that the Authority/Redesign program designate the successor; the refactor pass can only mark the reference as dangling.

The whitelist can flag and repair the cross-reference target (RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE), but it cannot supply the correct live authority to substitute, because that authority does not appear in the excerpted source texts. Identifying and validating the current FDICIA statutory/regulatory provision that grounds OBL-4 is an evidentiary/research task outside the refactor whitelist and outside the excerpt boundary; it should be logged for the Authority (or Redesign Backlog) as a source-supply action rather than improvised here.

The whitelist cannot express this fix cleanly. SUBSTITUTE-TERM is constrained to be STRICTLY meaning-preserving, but resolving the abolished-OTS reference requires selecting among multiple Dodd-Frank successor agencies (OCC/FDIC/Board), which is a substantive determination the excerpted sources do not settle. There is no whitelist move for 'update an obsolete actor reference to a policy-chosen successor.' This should be logged as a finding recommending an ADR (or Redesign Backlog routing) to authorize a non-meaning-preserving successor-actor substitution; it must not be improvised as a meaning-preserving rename. Additionally, the (h) subsection quoted in the defect does not appear in the SOURCE TEXT EXCERPTS provided (the excerpt ends at subsection (e)), so the verbatim-quote and successor-identification work cannot be completed on the record available and should be flagged for source re-extraction.

The defect's core is a MISSING duty: no instrument states a required detection latency for fast-moving runs. The whitelist can only make explicit a duty the sources already establish (INTRODUCE per ADR-005), and no source establishes an affirmative near-real-time liquidity monitoring or detection-latency obligation — the FR 2052a purpose language ('timely information on firm-specific liquidity risks during periods of stress') describes a data-collection aim, not a stated detection-speed duty on any actor. Proposing an INTRODUCE here would create a NEW duty, which ADR-005 forbids softening but which is genuinely absent from the sources; the honest path is to log this as a substantive gap for the Redesign Backlog rather than manufacture the obligation via a refactor move. The RELATE-OBLIGATION above surfaces the gap at blueprint level; closing it requires a policy choice (setting a latency standard) that exceeds a meaning-preserving refactor and belongs to the separately chartered Principal-led redesign program named in the ratified scope.

D9 is a genuine gap defect, not a drawing defect, and the P3.1 whitelist cannot express it honestly at the refactor level. The whitelist moves all operate on material the sources already contain: MERGE/SPLIT/RELOCATE/NORMALIZE-ELEMENTS reorganize existing elements; CANONICALIZE-DEFINITION/DEFINE-TERM/SUBSTITUTE-TERM operate on terms present in the texts; RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE/RELATE-OBLIGATION link existing obligations; ELEVATE-GENERAL-RULE/FACTOR-EXCEPTION restructure existing rules. None of these can supply an obligation concerning Call Report or FR 2052a reporting timing/granularity, because — as the defect finding records and the extractions confirm — no such obligation exists anywhere in the three extracted instruments. The cfp-addendum-2023 text addresses only contingency funding plans, funding-source diversity, operational readiness, and discount-window access; it never mentions Call Reports or FR 2052a. The occ-bulletin-2023-25 text is a transmittal summary whose fullest reporting-adjacent content is that banks should 'understand requirements and maintain operational readiness to borrow from federal funding facilities, such as the Federal Reserve discount window, if these facilities are part of their contingency funding plans' — nothing on reporting instruments. INTRODUCE is the only candidate, but ADR-005 confines INTRODUCE to making explicit a duty the sources ALREADY establish. A duty to report liquidity in a run-relevant timeframe via Call Report/FR 2052a is not latent in these three sources — it is absent from them. So INTRODUCE here would not be making-explicit; it would be authoring a new duty from the diagnostic's implication ('the obligation ... is implied by the diagnostic structure but stated nowhere in these sources'). Per ADR-005 the honest path is to name that this is a new duty and route it to the Redesign Backlog rather than manufacture it under an INTRODUCE label pointed at sources that do not support it. This is also consistent with the refactor-pass constraint (fix the drawing, not the bricks): the reporting-timing obligation is a missing brick, and the ratified scope for THIS program is explicitly to build 'the evidentiary foundation on which a future, separately chartered, Principal-led redesign program can be convened' — i.e., to register the gap, not to close it. Recommendation: log D9 as a Redesign Backlog item flagging (a) that the run-relevant reporting-timing/granularity obligation is a substantive gap across all extracted instruments, and (b) that closing it requires source instruments not yet in scope (the Call Report and FR 2052a authorities themselves), whose ingestion is a scoping decision for the chartered redesign program, not a refactor move. No verified verbatim citation can support an affirmative operation because the supporting spans do not exist in these texts; that absence is itself the finding.

The second half of D9 — the absence of any obligation on the Reserve Bank to COMMUNICATE the assigned collateral value or margin back to the pledging institution — cannot be resolved by the whitelist. INTRODUCE is barred here because the sources establish no such duty even implicitly: the source states values are 'assigned' and 'used by the Reserve Bank' and directs institutions to 'contact their local Reserve Bank' with questions, which points the informational flow the other way. There is no consequence in the sources that presupposes a Reserve Bank notification duty (unlike the supply-of-information duty, which is presupposed by the zero-value consequence). A duty to notify assigned value/margin would be genuinely new operative substance, not a refactor of existing drawing, and no meaning-preserving move expresses it. This should be logged as a finding for the Redesign Backlog (candidate new-duty proposal), not improvised here.

The defect's root remedy — a stated obligation or channel by which FHFA actually OBTAINS member examination reports — cannot be honestly expressed by any whitelist move. The source establishes NO such duty: it states only that reports are 'not directly available' and that FHFA has 'initiated discussions' to improve information exchange. INTRODUCE is barred by ADR-005 because making such a channel explicit would create a new duty, not surface an existing one; the 'discussions' language is an activity description, not an established obligation, and treating it as one would fabricate a channel the sources do not confer. RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE does not apply because there is no dangling reference to a channel — the channel simply does not exist in the sources. This is therefore a substantive gap for the Redesign Backlog: the future Principal-led program must decide whether to charter an examination-report access mechanism. The RELATE-OBLIGATION move above makes the gap visible; it does not close it, and no whitelist move can close it without improvising legal substance in violation of ADR-003 and ADR-005.

This defect is a scope-coverage gap, not a drawing error the P3.1 whitelist can fix. The whitelist operates on elements that EXIST in the sources/extractions (MERGE, SPLIT, RELOCATE, CANONICALIZE-DEFINITION, etc.) or makes explicit a duty the sources ALREADY establish (INTRODUCE, per ADR-005). Here, both extractions affirmatively record that FHLB collateral/operational rules, Call Reports, and FR 2052a are ABSENT from the underlying sources (the Hsu and McKernan speeches). The refactor pass fixes the drawing, not the bricks: no whitelist move can conjure coverage of a topic that neither source addresses, because there is no source-established duty, definition, term, or cross-reference to merge, relocate, canonicalize, or make explicit. INTRODUCE is unavailable because the missing coverage is not a duty latent in these two sources; sourcing it would require bringing in the actual FHLB/Call Report/FR 2052a instruments (e.g., FHFA collateral rules, FFIEC 031/041, the FR 2052a reporting form) as new source material, which is an acquisition/scoping action for the diagnostic's evidentiary base, not a blueprint refactor. Verbatim confirmation that the sources do not reach these topics: Hsu closes on 'faster payments and tokenization' and the discount window without touching FHLB or the reporting instruments, and McKernan's own frame is 'operational readiness and discount window stigma need a better solution' — quote: 'almost everyone now agrees that operational readiness and discount window stigma need a better solution.' Recommended routing: log this to the source-acquisition / scoping backlog for the diagnostic (identify and excerpt the FHLB and liquidity-reporting instruments the ratified scope names), NOT the P3.2 refactor queue. No improvised move is proposed.

The core of D9 — an actual interoperability/cross-reference bridge between Reg A collateral/operational rules and the FHLB collateral/operational regime — cannot be expressed by the P3.1 whitelist within this single-source refactor. RESOLVE-CROSS-REFERENCE requires an existing (broken or ambiguous) cross-reference to resolve; here the FHLB rules are cited only for the membership definition, and no cross-reference to FHLB collateral/operational provisions exists to repair. Creating a genuine two-regime interoperability provision is a substantive coordination duty spanning documents not both in scope, which exceeds a meaning-preserving drawing fix. This is a logged finding recommending an ADR (and Redesign-program treatment): whether and how the Fed discount-window and FHLB collateral regimes should be made interoperable is a policy choice for the future Principal-led redesign, not a refactor move.

The core of D9 — a provision governing the TIMING and GRANULARITY of liquidity reporting (Call Reports, FR 2052a) tied to discount-window lending decisions — cannot be expressed by any P3.1 whitelist move, because no such duty exists in the Reg A source to make explicit. INTRODUCE under ADR-005 is limited to duties the sources already establish; Reg A establishes only that Reserve Banks must keep informed and obtain evidence, not any cadence or data-granularity obligation on the reporting instruments themselves. Creating a timing/granularity reporting duty would be a genuinely NEW obligation and must be routed to the Redesign Backlog rather than fabricated as a refactor. Additionally, FR 2052a and Call Reports are governed by instruments outside this item_id; relating Reg A to a reporting-cadence rule that does not exist in-scope is a cross-item design choice for the future Principal-led redesign program, not a meaning-preserving refactor. Logging as a candidate ADR: whether the redesign should introduce a liquidity-reporting timing/granularity provision anchored to discount-window decisions.
